title: Why Root Canals Have a Painful Reputation (and the Reality Today)
metaTitle: Root Canal Myths: The Painful Reputation vs Reality
metaDescription: Why do root canals have such a bad reputation, and is it still deserved? We separate the myths from the reality of modern root canal treatment today.
excerpt: Root canals carry a fearsome reputation, but much of it is rooted in the past. Here is where the myth comes from and what modern treatment is really like.
heroImageAlt: A thoughtful patient reading about dental treatment in a calm clinic setting.
bodyHtml:
Where the fearsome reputation comes from

Ask almost anyone about root canals and you will hear the same thing: they are the thing to dread. Yet the reality today is that, for most people, a root canal feels similar to having a filling placed, with modern local anaesthetic doing the heavy lifting. The gap between the reputation and the experience is one of the widest in dentistry — and it exists for understandable reasons. Much of the dread is inherited from a time before today's anaesthetics and techniques, and much of it is really a memory of the toothache that led to treatment, not the treatment itself.

It is worth untangling the myths, because fear of the procedure keeps some people from dealing with a problem that only gets harder to manage the longer it waits.

Myth: "The root canal is what hurts"

In most cases, the pain people associate with a root canal came before the appointment. A tooth that needs root canal treatment is often already inflamed or infected, and the nerve inside is sensitive and enclosed in a rigid space, which can produce intense, lingering pain. The procedure is designed to remove that inflamed tissue and address the source of the ache. Many people actually feel relief in the days after treatment, once healing begins. Blaming the root canal for the pain is a bit like blaming the fire brigade for the fire.

Myth: "Nothing can make it comfortable"

The old reputation took hold in an era with fewer tools for comfort. Today, local anaesthetic reliably numbs the tooth for the large majority of people, and dentists have additional techniques for teeth that are harder to freeze. During treatment you typically feel pressure and vibration rather than sharp pain, and you can raise your hand to pause at any time. This is the single biggest reason the modern experience does not match the scary stories.

Myth: "It's better to just pull the tooth"

Extraction can seem like the simpler escape, but removing a tooth is not the end of the story — it raises the separate question of how to replace it to keep your bite and neighbouring teeth healthy. Where a tooth can be saved, keeping your natural tooth is often the preferred path. Which option is right depends on your particular situation, and that is a conversation to have with your dentist rather than a decision driven by fear.

The reality of modern treatment

  • The area is numbed before anything begins, and your dentist checks that you are comfortable.
  • You will feel pressure and movement, which are normal, rather than sharp pain.
  • Mild soreness for a few days afterward is common and usually eases with over-the-counter pain relief.
  • You remain in control and can ask to pause whenever you need to.

If it's so routine now, why the lasting fear?

Reputations outlive the reality that created them. Frightening stories are memorable and get repeated, while uneventful appointments rarely make for a dramatic tale. Add the real pain of a bad toothache into the mix, and it is easy to see why the myth persists even as the experience has changed.

Should I be worried if I'm nervous?

Nervousness is completely normal, and a good dental team expects it. Telling them you are anxious lets them explain each step, go at your pace, and agree on a signal to pause. Understanding what will happen is one of the most reliable antidotes to dread.

Does a painful reputation mean I should delay?

Generally the opposite is true. A tooth that needs treatment tends to become more uncomfortable and more complicated the longer it is left. Acting sooner often means a smoother, more comfortable visit.

Letting the facts replace the fear

If an old reputation has been shaping your expectations, it may help to hear what treatment actually involves from a dentist directly. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, provides root canal treatment at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, where you can ask questions before deciding anything. You can also read more about root canal therapy at the Markham clinic.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
